sections.title: Step size is a dial, not a detail
paragraphs: After a {{model}} computes {{loss}}, training nudges each {{weights}} value a little. How far that nudge travels is the {{learningRate}}.
Picture walking downhill in fog. Tiny steps keep you safe but take forever. Giant leaps might leap past the valley floor and climb the other side.
The {{gradient}} points downhill. The {{learningRate}} scales how far you move along that direction in one update.
Same {{loss}} formula, same data, different {{learningRate}}: training can crawl, converge or thrash. The dial belongs inside the training loop, next to {{weights}} and {{bias}}.
You already saw {{learningRate}} named in Loss and updates. This lesson makes the dial the main idea before you open Bias and weights.
bullets: Too large or too small both waste training time.

check.prompt: Training {{loss}} jumps up and down every step with no steady drop. What is the most likely inside cause among these options?
check.answer: Learning rate is too large and updates overshoot
choices: Learning rate is too large and updates overshoot
check.explanation: Huge steps along the {{gradient}} often overshoot the low-{{loss}} region, so {{loss}} bounces. Turning the {{learningRate}} down is the first fix to try inside the training loop.

sections.title: Too small, too large, just workable
paragraphs: A tiny {{learningRate}} makes each update almost invisible. {{loss}} may fall, but only after many {{epoch}}s. Teams sometimes mistake that crawl for a broken {{model}}.
A huge {{learningRate}} can send {{weights}} into wild values. Predictions flip, {{loss}} explodes or oscillates and the run looks random.
A workable rate shrinks {{loss}} smoothly across early {{epoch}}s without fireworks. You still check a held-out set later; a pretty training curve is not proof of {{generalization}}.
Click each story to connect it to the dial. The optional Learning rate lab lets you watch tiny, medium and huge rates on the same toy bowl.
Real optimizers add momentum and adaptive rates. The teaching point stays: step size is part of what happens inside training, not a UI decoration.

reveals.prompt: {{loss}} barely moves after hundreds of steps.
reveals.reveal: Often the {{learningRate}} is too small. Try a larger step before redesigning the whole network.
Often the {{learningRate}} is too large. Cut it and restart from sane {{weights}}.

reveals.prompt: {{loss}} falls for a while then plateaus.
reveals.reveal: Normal late training. Confirm on held-out data; do not keep cranking the rate forever.

check.prompt: You want a first teaching run on XOR. Which {{learningRate}} habit matches this lesson?
check.answer: Start moderate, watch loss, then adjust the dial
choices: Start moderate, watch loss, then adjust the dial
Always use the largest rate the hardware allows
Set learning rate to zero so weights never change
Ignore learning rate because only architecture matters
check.explanation: Inside training, the {{learningRate}} is a {{hyperparameters}} you tune by watching {{loss}} behavior. Moderate first, then adjust with evidence from the curve.

sections.title: From dial to neuron parts
paragraphs: Once step size makes sense, the next question is what those numbers are. Each neuron stores {{weights}} on its inputs and a {{bias}} offset.
Training multiplies the {{gradient}} by the {{learningRate}} and subtracts that product from each {{weights}} entry (and the {{bias}}). That is the update you will see in Bias and weights.
Keep one mental checklist: data in, forward {{prediction}}, {{loss}}, {{gradient}}, scaled step, new {{weights}}. The dial sits in the middle of that checklist.
Honesty: production stacks pick schedules that decay the {{learningRate}} over time. The lab uses fixed rates so you can see the effect clearly.
Next lesson: **Bias and weights**, where you inspect the numbers the dial is moving. Try the optional Learning rate lab if you want a hands-on bowl before you go.
bullets: Next spine lesson: Bias and weights.
Optional lab: compare tiny, medium and huge rates.

aside.title: Practice the dial
aside.body: Open the Learning rate lab and compare how tiny, medium and huge rates move the same toy {{loss}} bowl.

check.prompt: In one short phrase, where does {{learningRate}} sit in the training checklist?
check.answer: It scales the gradient step on weights
accept: multiplies the gradient for the update
controls size of each weight nudge
check.explanation: The {{learningRate}} does not replace {{loss}} or the {{gradient}}. It scales how far each update moves the {{weights}} (and {{bias}}) inside the model.

recapQuestions.prompt: Which failure matches a {{learningRate}} that is much too large?
recapQuestions.answer: Loss oscillates or explodes as updates overshoot
choices: Loss oscillates or explodes as updates overshoot
The model refuses to tokenize text
recapQuestions.explanation: Overshooting the low-{{loss}} region is the classic large-rate failure inside training. Shrink the dial and watch the curve again.

recapQuestions.prompt: Complete the idea: the {{learningRate}} is best described as…
recapQuestions.answer: The step size on each weight update
accept: how far weights move each step
recapQuestions.explanation: Keep the inside meaning crisp: {{learningRate}} is the step size applied when {{weights}} move along the {{gradient}}.
